title: Paula Poundstone
location: Buskirk-Chumley Theater,114 East Kirkwood Avenue, Bloomington, IN 47408, USA
description:
Iconic comedian Paula Poundstone is known for her smart, observational humor and a spontaneous wit that has become the stuff of legend. She regularly plays theaters across the country, hosts a weekly comedy podcast, Nobody Listens to Paula Poundstone, and is a regular panelist on NPR’s Wait, Wait… Don’t Tell Me. She also voiced the character ‘Forgetter Paula’ in the feature films Inside Out and Inside Out 2.

Paula has starred in several HBO specials, including Cats, Cops and Stuff, which nabbed a cable ACE award for Best Comedy Special. She was the first female comic to host the White House Correspondents Dinner. She filmed live coverage of the 1992 Democratic and Republican National Conventions and the Presidential Inaugural for The Tonight Show with Jay Leno and at the 93rd Emmy Awards. Paula has starred in two television series, both entitled The Paula Poundstone Show.

Paula’s second book, The Totally Unscientific Study of the Search for Human Happiness, was one of eight semi-finalists for the Thurber Prize for American Humor; the audiobook was one of five finalists for the AUDIE award for Audiobook of the Year.

Paula has released five albums and is featured in several documentaries and compendiums noting influential comedians of our time.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

Featuring musicians who play boogie-woogie, blues, and related styles in free and ticketed performances, Bloomington Boogies strives to introduce young people to artists and various non-classical styles through public concerts and free educational activities, including school performances, workshops, and master classes.

The festival begins with free performances throughout the day on Saturday, Oct. 10th:

title: New Moon Hike, Brown County State Park
location: Brown County State Park, Park office, 1405 S.R. 46 W, Nashville, IN
description: Full Moons occur when the Moon is fully illuminated by the Sun, allowing viewers on Earth to see the full circle. It's typically the brightest night of the month. The New Moon is the darkest night of the month, when dark side of the Moon faces Earth. We're going on a hike on the darkest night of the month! We will meet at the Park Office/Fire Tower Parking lot at 7:30pm to hike Trail 10. Please note Trail 10 should be considered very rugged in the dark and involves hiking from one of the highest elevations in the park to one of the lowest. The route is 2.2 miles and will take about two hours. Red flashlights help us preserve night vision. We have some to lend out, but it is wise to bring your own if you have one. Hike cancellation policy: Hikes will be cancelled if there is lightning, temperatures below 0 degrees Farenheit, temperature indexes above 105 degrees Farenheit, or a wind advisory. If a hike is cancelled, gatehouses will be informed. The phone number for the North Gatehouse is 812-988-5230.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

description: Join the Borns Jewish Studies Program for the opening symposium of Memory Transformed: Materials of Heritage in Jewish Eastern European Life, a day of scholarship, art, and music exploring how Eastern European Jewish culture is remembered and continues to shape contemporary artistic production.11:00 a.m. — Complimentary Brunch at the Tudor Room*The complimentary brunch at the Tudor Room is currently at capacity. If space becomes available, registered attendees will be contacted.*12:30–3:00 p.m. — SymposiumDogwood Room, Indiana Memorial Union  The symposium will feature two panels examining Jewish material culture, music, memory, and the cultural afterlives of objects associated with Eastern European Jewish life. Scholars and artists will explore how recordings, photographs, books, memorials, and other cultural objects preserve knowledge, shape memory, and inspire contemporary cultural production.Panel 1Judith BerksonPatterns of Improvisation in Live Cantorial Recordings, 1950–1980Jeremiah LockwoodPlastinkes and idisher rekords: Towards a History of Jewish Sacred Pop Music as Material CultureDov-Ber KerlerFrom the New to the Old World and Vice Versa: Contrafacts, Adaptation and Radical ReworkingPanel 2Halina GoldbergMaterial Culture, Memory, and the Making of a Museum and Digital Project on Jewish ŁódźNicolette van den BogerdComposing Jewish Musical Material Culture After the HolocaustJennifer McComasTransformations of Material and Memory in Ruth Weinberg's Shtetl PortfolioModerators  Joanna Niżyńska  Sergio Ospina-Romero  The symposium is part of the larger Memory Transformed program taking place throughout the day on Sunday, October 11, including brunch, an afternoon reception and optional guided museum tours at the Eskenazi Museum of Art, and an evening concert at Auer Hall.Free and open to the public. Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana. title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Center for Refugee Studies Op-Ed Initiative Webinar Series
description: The CRS Op-Ed Initiative, open to faculty, students, and the CRS community, teaches participants how to convert research insights into accessible, public-facing op-eds. This four-course series covers how to develop, write, edit, and publish op-eds, and why opinion writing is an important vessel for spreading innovative ideas and sparking important discussions. Participants do not need any prior publication experience to join, and the course is free.The series is led by Assistant Director Meredith Perkins, who has six years of experience writing over 50 op-eds as a freelance journalist in student, local, and national publications. She won the 2024 and 2025 Region 4 Society of Professional Journalists Best College Opinion Writing award and the 2023 Ohio News Media Association Best Collegiate Column Writing award. A current Master of Public Affairs-Master of International Affairs student, her past newsroom experience inspires her to make complex academic conversations accessible for public audiences.Session 1: Before You Writewill introduce the history and purpose of op-eds and the range of places where opinion writing appears, including local and national newspapers, industry publications, departmental blogs, and platforms such as Substack. We will review genre conventions of op-eds, why op-eds are useful, and what information writers should know (e.g. workplace media policies) before considering publication.Session 2: Drafting Your First Op-Edwill focus on identifying a strong and timely argument. Participants will examine who is already writing about their topic, the dominant conversation surrounding it, and recent news or research that might create an opportunity for commentary. A central exercise will help participants identify the "knowledge gap" between what they know through expertise, research, or lived experience and what a general reader is likely to know. Participants will use that gap to develop a clear, relevant argument for a public audience.Session 3: Editing Your Op-Edwill help participants turn a draft into an accessible, publication-ready piece. Topics will include common word-count requirements, clear and concise language, reducing jargon, checking hyperlinks and sources, anticipating possible misunderstandings, proper image attribution, headline writing, and basic search engine optimization. After the session, participants can send drafts to the instructor for personalized feedback.Session 4: Publishing and Pitching Your Op-Edwill help participants identify the right outlet for their work based on the audience they hope to reach. The session will compare features and challenges of publishing in local and national newspapers, industry publications, institutional blogs, and independent platforms. Participants will learn what to include in a submission or pitch, such as a brief description, author bio, word count, contact information, and headshot, as well as how to recognize potential red flags. The session will conclude with an editor's perspective on what happens behind the inbox, including high submission volume, response times, competition for limited space, and why many submissions may be read without receiving a reply.By the end of the series, participants should understand how to identify a compelling op-ed idea, communicate specialized knowledge to a general audience, edit a piece to common publication standards, and develop a realistic strategy for publication. Participants who work on a piece throughout the program may leave with a completed or near-completed op-ed and a list of appropriate outlets to approach.       Register to attend at https://go.iu.edu/cVZV1S (https://go.iu.edu/cVZV1S) to get the Zoom link.

title: Jazz @ the BCT: Natalie Boeyink Jazz Ensemble
description: Enjoy this performance from almost anywhere in the world viaLIVE@jacobs!About the DirectorNatalie Boeyink, bassist and educator, serves as associate professor of music jazz studies at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. After earning her doctorate in music education at the Jacobs School in 2015, Boeyink spent eight years as a jazz lecturer and senior lecturer in the University of North Carolina system. She earned an M.M. in Jazz Performance at the University of Louisville and a B.M. in Jazz Studies at Jacobs. Her interest in the educational experiences and careers of jazzwomen has launched a series of research projects, conference presentations and publications, including her dissertation, "An Analysis and Description of Female Jazz Instrumentalists." An advocate for jazzwomen, Boeyink served as chair of the Jazz Education Network's Women in Jazz Committee and worked to reestablish the Sisters in Jazz Collegiate Combo Competition. Batuquê Trio is Boeyink's seasoned collaboration with drummer Andy Smith and pianist Jamaal Baptiste. Focusing on contemporary Brazilian, Afro-Cuban, and Caribbean jazz, the trio frequently appears at jazz festivals as performers and clinicians. Their first CD, Transparency, was released in 2015. A second album is forthcoming in 2024. Some of Boeyink's notable performances include appearances with Tammy McCann, Jamie Baum, Ingrid Jensen, Terri Lyne Carrington, Christine Jensen, Leni Stern, Jovino Santos Neto, Joe Piscopo, David "Fathead" Newman, Jon Hendricks, Jeff Coffin, David Liebman, and Lorraine Feather. Meeting URL: https://liveatjacobs.music.indiana.edu/

title: Be a Part of the"Day in My Life"Series
Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Fall 2026 CLACS Faculty Research Symposium with Luis A. González
description: CLACS Faculty Research Symposium welcomes Luis A. González, Librarian for Latin American, Spanish & Portuguese, Latino, and European Studies, and an Adjunct faculty in History at Indiana University as he presents: Books in Formerly Sacred Spaces: The Story of a Public Library, a President, and an Artist — Jiquilpan, Mexico, 1941   Abstract:  This presentation considers the Gabino Ortiz Public Library, notably founded by President Lázaro Cárdenas in his hometown of Jiquilpan, Michoacán, in 1941. As part of his national cultural project, President Cárdenas opened the library within a repurposed church which also houses murals by José Clemente Orozco depicting events from the Mexican Revolution. This case study presents a compelling opportunity to examine the intersections of state cultural policy, collective memory, and the social imaginary of the library in modern Mexico.   Biography:  Luis A. González is the Librarian for Latin American, Spanish & Portuguese, Latino, and European Studies, and an Adjunct faculty in History at Indiana University. He has published in the fields of Brazilian agrarian, social, and socio-legal history, and in Latin American Studies librarianship. Luis is a Contributing Editor for the Handbook of Latin American Studies, published by the Hispanic Division of the Library of Congress, and past president of the Seminar on the Acquisition of Latin American Library Materials (SALALM).

title: Chinese Tidings: "The Belt and Road Initiative: Domestic Policymaking and Global Impacts"
description: Pizza is served at 5:30 pm. and the lecture starts at 6:00 pm.About the lecture: Launched in 2013, the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) occupies a central position in China's contemporary foreign policy and domestic development  agenda. While often described as an infrastructure investment program, the BRI encompasses multiple dimensions of development policymaking, trade and investment facilitation, financial cooperation, and people-to-people exchange. Understanding how the initiative is organized and implemented is crucial for making sense of China's evolving position in the global economic and political system. This lecture provides a framework for understanding the BRI, with particular attention to its domestic organizing mechanisms, how they shape China's engagement with partner countries, and the broader implications of the initiative for global development.About the presenter: Dr. Hong Zhang is an Assistant Professor in the Department of International Studies at the Hamilton Lugar School. Her research focuses on the political economy of global development and China's role in it. She teaches courses on global development, infrastructure, and China–Global South relations. She is currently writing a book on China's developmental statecraft, examining how  China builds structural power in the global economy while strengthening its  developmental state at home.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

description: Outfitting IU Athletics: Hoosier Champions                  This exhibit showcases objects from IU's championship teams and athletes, connecting them to historic achievements in the Big Ten and the national stage. The items featured in the exhibit are from the IU Athletics Sports Memorabilia Collection and feature photos and videos provided by IU Athletics and Indiana University Archives.                Dates: November 14, 2025 - October 2026                                      By Their Own Hands: The Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame!          Founded in 1974 by the Culture and Ethnic Affairs Guild of the Oakland Museum of California, the Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame began as a film lecture series and awards ceremony celebrating achievements of Black film industry figures. When that organization closed, they donated their materials to IU. In collaboration with the IU Black Film Center and Archive, this exhibit features objects from that collection, including founding documents, costumes, and handprints of inductees to the Hall of Fame.        Dates: September 2025 - December 2026                                      Capturing the Campus: T.C. Steele, Indiana University's First Artist in ResidenceCapturing the Campus pays tribute to renowned Hoosier artist T.C. Steele. The exhibit honors the century that has passed since his death by showcasing paintings form the artist's residency at IU and other relevant works. The exhibit will bring together Steele's landscapes from the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection and the Indiana State Museum and Historic Sites' collection, allowing the holdings of these two collections to be viewed in one space.        Dates: April 17, 2026 - April 2026                   Multipurpose Room          Currently Featuring: The Gift of Collecting: Tina Jernigan          Jernigan was a passionate supporter of both Indiana University and the arts. She donated artworks to the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection upon her passing in 2024. With funding provided by Jernigan, Public Art professionally framed, hung, and preserved these pieces for this exhibit in the McCalla Building and for future installations on campus.         Dates: July 2026-July 2027

title: Ostrom Workshop | Research Series: Diego Pacheco
location: The Ostrom Workshop, 513 N PARK AVE
description: Bio  Diego Pacheco Balanza is a Bolivian researcher, public policy specialist, and former diplomat with over two decades of experience in sustainable development, environmental governance, and international negotiations. He holds a Ph.D. in Public Policy from Indiana University, where he studied under Nobel Laureate Elinor Ostrom, an MSc in Rural Resources and Environmental Policy from Imperial College London, and a BA in Anthropology.  His work has focused on the relationships between society and Nature, institutional governance, Indigenous Peoples, climate change, biodiversity, and the development of the Living Well (Vivir Bien) approach and cosmobiocentric perspectives for sustainability. Most recently, he served as Director General for Living Well and Foreign Policy at the Office of the Vice President of the Plurinational State of Bolivia and as Chargé d'Affaires a.i. at the Permanent Mission of Bolivia to the United Nations in New York. He has also served twice as Bolivia's Vice Minister of Planning and represented the country in multilateral environmental negotiations under the UNFCCC, CBD, and IPBES. He is the author of numerous books and scientific publications on public policy, Mother Earth, natural resources governance and sustainable development. His current research explores new pathways for global governance through the integration of indigenous knowledge, collective action, and Mother Earth-centered approaches.Title  From Social–Ecological Systems toward Life Systems: Expanding Ostromian Institutional Analysis toward Mother Earth FuturesAbstract  Building on the growing recognition of Indigenous and local knowledge systems, plural worldviews, and relational approaches to human–Nature relationships, this talk explores how the Ostrom Workshop tradition of institutional analysis and collective action theory might be expanded to engage these non-anthropocentric perspectives. It considers a shift from an analytical focus on human actors as the primary agents of collective action within social–ecological systems toward Communities of Life within Life Systems, and introduces an analytical framework and empirical architecture for examining Human–Mother Earth co-flourishing. This also speaks to an emerging research gap concerning the joint examination of human and more-than-human outcomes, rather than treating their relationship predominantly in one direction.About the Ostrom Workshop Research Series  Learn about innovative research by Graduate Students and Visiting Scholars as they advance the mission of the Ostrom Workshop, building upon the theme of governance to understand and address major societal problems.

title: Ballet Hispánico New York
description: Ballet Hispánico New York is the nation's leading American Latino dance company and the largest cultural institution of its kind in the United States. For over five decades, it has been a beacon of artistic excellence, celebrated for its bold repertory and exceptional training programs.     The Bloomington performance will be an evening-length presentation of CARMEN.maquia. Since the debut in 1875, Carmen, the titular character from Bizet's opera, has become a timeless cultural icon, inspiring generations of composers, choreographers, and writers to attempt to capture her elusive and alluring nature.     Ballet Hispnico honors the powerful Spanish leading lady with Gustavo Ramírez Sansano's electrifying CARMEN.maquia. One of today's most sought-after choreographers, Sansano's quintessential ballet invigorates this timeless tale with an unrelenting energy that leaves you breathless. Highly original and full of explosive movement, CARMEN.maquia is a bold reimagining of this tragic tale.

title: Émile Naoumoff, piano
description: Featuring the slow movements of Mozart's piano concertos K.453, K.467, K.491, K.271, and K.488About the ArtistÉmile Naoumoff is professor of music in piano at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music, where he has been on faculty since 1998. He has been likened to both Vladimir Horowitz and Arthur Rubinstein as a pianist, displaying, as one critic remarked, the fire of the former and the poetry of the latter. He revealed himself as a musical prodigy at age five, playing the piano and adding composition to his studies a year later. At age seven, he became the last disciple of Nadia Boulanger, who referred to him as "the gift of my old age." At age 18, he was signed by music publisher Schott, Mainz. Naoumoff studied with Boulanger until her death, permitting him also to work with Clifford Curzon, Igor Markevitch, and Robert and Gaby Casadesus, among others. Yehudi Menuhin conducted the premiere of Naoumoff's first piano concerto, with him as soloist, when Noumoff was 10 years old. Naoumoff pursued studies at the Paris Conservatory with Lelia Gousseau, Pierre Sancan, and Geneviève Joy, as well as at the École Normale de Musique de Paris with Pierre Dervaux (conducting). Upon Boulanger's death, he assumed her classes at the summer sessions of the Conservatoire d'Art Americain (Fontainebleau). He was later appointed to the Conservatoire National Supérieur de Musique, Paris. Naoumoff is regularly invited to perform by the world's premier orchestras, including the Los Angeles Philharmonic, Berlin Symphony, and Vienna Symphony, among many others. He has worked closely with such conductors as Leonard Bernstein, Leonard Slatkin, and Mstislav Rostropovich. He has also collaborated with a host of noteworthy musicians, including Jean-Pierre Rampal, Gerard Souzay, and Yo-Yo Ma. Naoumoff has been invited to perform at numerous music festivals, such as the Santander Summer Masterclasses, Verbier Academy Festival, Banff Center, and residencies at the Conservatory of Barcelona. He is an avid composer of French mélodies and is known for his transcriptions for the piano. He maintains a video journal of daily improvisations on his YouTube channel.

title: Be a Part of the"Day in My Life"Series
Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: HIV/STI Testing
description: Free HIV Testing & Safer Sex Supplies at the LGBTQ+ Culture Center  Taking care of your sexual health is an important part of your overall well-being, and we're committed to making resources accessible, welcoming, and judgment-free.Positive Link (https://iuhealth.org/find-medical-services/positive-link-hiv-services) provides free and confidential HIV testing in Room 204 of the LGBTQ+ Culture Center every Thursday from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. during the academic year. During the summer, testing is available on the first and third Thursdays of each month.  In addition, during the academic year, the Monroe County Health Department offers free chlamydia and gonorrhea testing on the third Thursday of every month, also from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. in Room 101.  The LGBTQ+ Culture Center also offers a variety of free safer sex supplies, including condoms, internal condoms, dental dams, lubricants, and educational materials on proper use. These resources are available to all students, free of charge. You can find them in the kitchenette area near the back entrance of the Center and are welcome to take what you need.  STI Testing & Safer Sex Resources Beyond Campus  Prioritizing your sexual health should be simple and accessible. In addition to services available at the LGBTQ+ Culture Center, students can receive testing on campus through the IU Student Health Center (https://healthcenter.indiana.edu/medical/sti-testing/index.html) or visit several local organizations (https://healthcenter.indiana.edu/health-answers/sexual-health/sti-testing-resources.html) that offer free or low-cost testing and prevention services.  Many of these providers offer confidential care, safer sex supplies, and supportive information about prevention, treatment, and sexual wellness. If you're unsure where to start, we're happy to help connect you with resources that fit your needs.All Indiana University events, groups, activities, educational, cultural, and historical observances welcome all members of the Indiana University community.

title: Scholarly Write-In
description:
Write and work in solidarity with other IU scholars. We offer a silent work environment with coffee and natural light. The write-in is open to all graduate students (at any stage of their degree program).

We will check in at the beginning of our meeting, set some goals together, then work independently for a few hours. Fifteen minutes prior to the close of the meeting, we will reconvene to update each other on our progress and set broad goals for the coming week.

This is a casual meeting – feel free to come for as much or as little time as you like, and only during the weeks that work for you. You are welcome and encouraged to work on anything that you need time and space for: participants regularly work on dissertations, course papers, syllabi and lesson plans, articles and pieces for publication, and grading. Our goal is to create a space where we can work together in solidarity on whatever projects we need to each week.

Meets weekly throughout the semester, Thursdays from 1-4pm. No meeting during Thanksgiving break.

Co-sponsored by Writing Tutorial Services and the IU Libraries.

title: Remembering the Climate Crisis
description: Presentation Abstract: Minority groups are more vulnerable to the impacts of climate change than the rest of the population. Latinx people are the largest growing minority in Indianapolis, yet little is known about how the local effects of climate change in the city impact this population. In this talk, Martell presents the preliminary findings of a study about how Latinx people in Indianapolis think about, feel, and remember climate change as well as their reactions to it. The goal is to develop policy recommendations and provide insights for future educational interventions about climate change education and advocacy.
source: IU La Casa Latino Cultural Center

description:
All are welcome to join the ACC in discussing Interpreter of Maladies, a 1999 short story collection by Indian-American author Jhumpa Lahiri.

title: Guest Music Theory Lecture – Jonathan De Souza (Western University, Ontario), "Music Theory and Practice: A Violin-Based Analysis of 'Salut d'amour'"
description: Abstract  Music theory has traditionally focused on abstract musical structures and idealized listeners. Yet in recent years, the discipline has increasingly considered performance, embodiment, instruments, and related issues. So, current theory engages practice. How can we think about this apparent paradigm shift? And more generally, about the relation between music theory and practice? In this talk, I'll approach these questions while developing an analysis of Edward Elgar's Salut d'amour, op. 12, that draws on my experience as a theorist and a lifelong violinist. Ultimately, I'll argue that theory and practice, like mind and body, are fundamentally interconnected.Five Friends Master Class Series – Honoring Robert SamelsThe Five Friends Master Class Series honoring the lives of five talented Jacobs School of Music students—Chris Carducci, Garth Eppley, Georgina Joshi, Zachary Novak, and Robert Samelswas established in 2012 with a gift of $1 million from the Georgina Joshi Foundation, Inc. This annual series of lectures, master classes, and residencies by a number of the world's leading musicians and teachers focuses on areas of interest most relevant to the lives of the five friends—voice performance, choral conducting, early music, music theory, composition, and opera. The Georgina Joshi Foundation was established in 2007 as the vision of Georgina Joshi's mother, Louise Addicott-Joshi, to provide educational and career development opportunities for young musicians and to encourage and support public performance of music. The gift to the school establishes a permanent way for the world to learn about each of the five friends, their musical talents and passions, and to encourage the development of similar talents and passions in current and future music students. The establishment of this endowment by the families is administered by the IU Foundation.  Bass-baritone and composer Robert Samels was born on June 2, 1981, and died in a plane crash on April 20, 2006. He was a doctoral student in choral conducting at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music and had studied voice with Giorgio Tozzi and Costanza Cuccaro. He began his vocal studies with Alfred Anderson at the University of Akron and Andreas Poulimenos at Bowling Green State University. Samels had recently appeared as Mr. Gibbs in the world premiere of Our Town by Ned Rorem, as Marco in the collegiate premiere of William Bolcom's A View from the Bridge, and as Joseph and Herod in the collegiate premiere of El Nino by John Adams. In September 2005, he conducted the premiere of his own opera, Pilatvs. As a member of the Wolf Trap Opera Company for 2006, he would have added three roles that summer, including Bartolo in Le Nozze di Figaro, Friar Laurence in Roméo et Juliette, and Pluto in Telemann's Orpheus. Other opera credits included the title roles of Don Pasquale and Il Turco in Italia, as well as Leporello in Don Giovanni, Falstaff in TheMerry Wives of Windsor, and Bottom in A Midsummer Night's Dream. In the summer of 2004, he performed Creon in the New York premiere of John Eaton's Antigone. Samels also frequently performed in the oratorio repertoire. In the spring of 2005, he was selected as a semi-finalist in the annual competition of the Oratorio Society of New York. He was an announcer with public radio station WFIU, as well as the host and producer of its Cantabile program. A soloist with Aguavá New Music Studio, he had recently performed a concert at the Library of Congress. Samels was an associate instructor in the Jacobs School's Music Theory Department, where was loved and admired by his students.
source: IU Jacobs School of Music, WFHB Community Calendar

title: AHS Speaker Series: William Chou on "Energy, Minerals, and the Race to Break China's Grip on Asia's Supply Chains"
description:
Powering the Alliance: Energy, Minerals, and the Race to Break China's Grip on Asia's Supply Chains
Dr. William Chou — Senior Fellow and Deputy Director, Japan Chair, Hudson Institute
China processes 90 percent of the world's rare earths and has twice cut off supply to Japan to win a political argument. It controls the inputs behind everything from electric vehicles to precision munitions. Dr. William Chou of the Hudson Institute explains how Beijing built that leverage, what it costs America and its allies, and what Washington and Tokyo are now spending hundreds of billions of dollars to undo. From Alaskan gas to rare earth magnets to the power plants behind the AI boom, this is the competition that will decide who sets the terms in the Indo-Pacific.
Hosted by the Alexander Hamilton Society at Indiana University. Free and open to the public.


Hosted by: The Alexander Hamilton Society at Indiana University 

Additional Information can be found at: https://beinvolved.indiana.edu/event/12803024

title: AHS/21JPSI: "Powering the Alliance: Energy, Minerals, and the Race to Break China's Grip on Asia's Supply Chains" (Dr. William Chou, Hudson Institute)
description: This public event is open to all students, faculty, staff, and members of the community. Please join us!  ———————————–About the talk:In recent years, Beijing has used its control over rare earth processing and energy inputs to pressure Japan, the U.S. and other trading partners. This talk will examine what has happened and discuss how the US and Japan are jointly responding, including a $550 billion strategic investment fund, Alaska LNG, allied mineral processing, and a power buildout to support the AI and semiconductor race. This event is hosted by the student-run Alexander Hamilton Society and co-sponsored by 21JPSI.About the speaker: William Chou is a senior fellow and deputy director of Hudson Institute's Japan Chair. His work at Hudson focuses on the United States' relationship with Japan and other Indo-Pacific issues, especially economic security, trade and investment, and regional partnerships. Dr. Chou's recent projects include analyses of the Nippon Steel–US Steel partnership, economic security cooperation among the US, Japan, and the European Union, automotive and critical mineral supply chains, and US industrial and trade initiatives around the world.  Dr. Chou writes and speaks regularly on policy issues, with his analysis appearing in publications such as The Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg, Politico, The Washington Post, Nikkei, The New York Times, and the Financial Times.  He holds a BA in history from Yale and a PhD in history from the Ohio State University, with a dissertation and book manuscript on Cold War US-Japan commercial and diplomatic relations. He is a former fellow at the Smithsonian, the Clements Center at the University of Texas at Austin, and the University of Tokyo. He began his career as a research analyst at the Institute for Defense Analyses during the Iraq War.All 21JPSI events are 100% in-person unless otherwise noted. This event is hosted by the student-run IU chapter of the Alexander Hamilton Society. 21JPSI is pleased to co-sponsor.
source: IU Hamilton Lugar School, IU Kelley School of Business

title: A Conversation with Bill Nye
description: Union Board, in collaboration with IU's College of Arts and Sciences, welcomes Bill Nye for a moderated Q&A at IU Auditorium. Best known to generations of viewers as "Bill Nye the Science Guy," Nye is an award-winning science educator, television presenter, mechanical engineer, author, and science advocate who has spent decades making science engaging and accessible to audiences of all ages.  He created and hosted the Emmy Award-winning PBS series Bill Nye the Science Guy and has continued his work in science communication through television, books, documentaries, and public speaking. He currently serves as Chief Ambassador and Vice Chairman of the Board of The Planetary Society, where he advocates for space exploration and planetary science.  During this special evening, Nye will participate in a moderated conversation exploring science, curiosity, education, space exploration, and his remarkable career. This event offers an opportunity to hear from one of the world's most recognizable science communicators and explore the questions that inspire him, getting to know the science television star on a more personal level.
